## Methods

Radar data observations
Radar data provides fine-scale convective structures and evolution processes at the kilometer scale with minute-level interval, making it the optimal observational dataset for studying the dynamic processes of hailstorm formation2. The hailstorm identification and classification in this work are determined by radar observations.

The mosaic radar observations in North America were obtained from Iowa State University Mesonet62 with a 5-minute temporal interval from April to August during 2015–2019. The radar data covers the continental United States of (66°–126° W, 24°–50° N) with 0.01° gird spacing.

The mosaic radar observations in East Asia were derived from radar images with a 6-minute temporal interval over South China from March to June during 2015–2019 and over East China from April to September during 2015–201926. The two regions cover (109.5°–117.5° E, 19.0°–26.1° N) and (112.0°–123.0° E, 28.0°–35.0° N) with a resolution of 0.01°, respectively.

Hailstorm identification and verification
Radar reflectivity increases sharply with the diameter of particle (Z~D6), hence pure rain rarely produces radar reflectivity exceeding 55 dBZ theoretically2,63. Therefore, the 55 dBZ threshold has been widely adopted as a key indicator for hailstorm and performs well around the world64-68. However, detecting hail signatures aloft does not guarantee the presence of hailstones at surface due to the melting process during descent. To address this, our study implements several measures to improve the robustness of hailstorm identification, as detailed below. Additionally, this research primarily focuses on the mechanisms of hailstorm formation pathway, rather than aiming for the precise identification of surface hailstones.

First, we raised the threshold from 55 dBZ to 60 dBZ. Previous studies indicated that this critical threshold effectively increases the surface hail validation to 93–97%69,70. We included only cases with at least 4 pixels (>4 km2) showing radar reflectivity exceeding 60 dBZ for more than two consecutive scans. These two criteria were implemented programmatically to identify potential hailstorms (programs and data are provided, please see the Code Availability section).

Subsequently, all results are manually reviewed to exclude highly organized convective systems such as tropical cyclones or squall lines. This is because these systems exhibit strong dynamical structures in which the hail particles are formed through a mechanism distinct from the merger-driven formation pathway.

Second, we verified the hailstorm identification results with surface hail reports from both climate regimes. For North America, we have collected all surface hail reports from Iowa Environmental Mesonet (https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/cow/) within the study areas in North America during the period from 2015 to 2019. Each record is plotted alongside radar reflectivity, considering only hail located within 20 km of convective systems (>40 dBZ) within a 10-minute time window. A total of 683 hailstorms (3,118 surface hail reports) were verified out of total 835 events, resulting in a verification ratio of 81.8%. The remaining 152 cases were examined, with their maximum radar reflectivity generally exceeding that of the verified cases (Supplementary Fig. 18). For East Asia, it is important to note that the comprehensive collection and immediate verification of hailstones at the surface present significant challenges, especially in remote areas that lack human inspections. We reviewed official media platforms from weather bureaus in South China and examined all records from 2015 to 2019. Among the 106 identified hailstorms, each was accompanied by severe weather warnings. Notably, 44 cases occurred within residential areas and were verified with photos and/or video evidence (Supplementary Fig. 19). There were 58 cases out of the remaining 62 cases transpired in remote locations, including mountains, forests, or water bodies, where immediate manual recording is not feasible. Additionally, four cases occurred in remote villages, where underdeveloped Internet and social networks may have hindered documentation, or residents may have lacked awareness of the need to record such events. Therefore, while public evidence supports approximately half of the cases, the absence of documentation in the remaining cases does not imply the absence of hail at the surface.

Third, we conduct cross-verification with another independent hydrometeor identification method based on polarimetric radar variables. The classified hail particles show a high degree of consistency with the results obtained from this method (purple pixels and 60 dBZ contours in Supplementary Figs. 10–11). Notably, the 60-dBZ method identifies smaller areas of hail particles compared to the polarimetric hydrometeor classification, indicating more stringent criteria and thereby reinforcing the robustness of the hailstorm identification results. In summary, the elevated thresholds and validations described above significantly enhance the credibility of this hailstorm detection method.

After verifications across two climate regimes described above, a total of 835 cases were identified in North America while 289 cases in East Asia.

Hailstorm tracking and classification
The hailstorm tracking algorithm is implemented after identifying the hail signal from radar reflectivity, specifically, when 4 pixels exceed 60 dBZ over a duration of at least 3 frames. The system’s moving direction and speed of movement are calculated based on the spatial similarity of consecutive frames, prior to the tracking and calculation. Subsequently, the hailstorm is spatially shifted to the center of a 200×200 km2 box, spanning from −3 to 3 hours relative to the first hail signal. Note that the cell-merger analysis focuses on intense convective cells with the potential to produce hail; therefore, convective cells in this study are defined as regions with radar reflectivity exceeding 40 dBZ. All related variables are thereby calculated within this box, including the location of hailstorm, the areal coverage of convection (>40 dBZ), and the area of hail (>60 dBZ), among others. The algorithm tracks the convective cell prior to the merger (defined as the contact of 40 dBZ contours between convective systems) and continues to track the larger one if a hailstorm causes a split, although such splits are very rare during our manual inspections.

The convective initiation and cell merger algorithms are applied to the 6-hour dataset established earlier. For convective initiation, we identify the potential convective cell at time t as Area_t, and then calculate the convective area within this cell coverage at time t-1. If Area_t-1 < 0.5 and Area_t < 4 pixel, the frequency of convective initiation is recorded. For cell merger, we compare the convection of two consecutive frames. If the previous one contains more than one convective cells according to connectivity principle, the cell merger process is considered to have occur. The logic diagrams for these algorithms are included in Supplementary Fig. 20. Additionally, the program and related data are provided in the Code Availability section.

Two formation pathways for hailstorms are identified based on whether the cell merger directly leads to their formation. Specifically, when the hailstone signature (radar reflectivity >60 dBZ) appeared within a half-hour window after a cell merger, this case is classified as a merger hailstorm. Otherwise, the hailstorms are categorized as normal hailstorms. Supplementary Fig. 1 provides the conceptual models for the evolution of these two types of hailstorms, along with observational examples. All classifications were initially pre-processed programmatically and then manually verified. Sensitivity tests of the storm-tracking algorithm and key threshold choices show strong consistency, with mean trajectory differences generally within 2% and maximum differences below 5%.

Urban area identification
The urban land cover data is obtained from the MODIS dataset. Notably, the urban normally has an impact on convective systems in metropolitan areas and downwind of city centers44,71,72. Therefore, we extend the urban-influencing region to an equivalent radius around the urban land cover, with this equivalent radius calculated from the original equivalent areal coverage for each isolated urban land cover73. This urban-influencing region and urban land cover together are termed as urban areas (UBA) in this work, and the rest are termed as rural-land regions (RUL). We have tested that the changes of influencing radius do not change the key conclusions of this work.

Environmental conditions and uncertainty estimate
The environmental conditions in Fig. 3 are averaged using the ERA5-Land and ERA5 reanalysis at the time of convective initiation (when maximal reflectivity exceeds 40 dBZ) for each hailstorm event. The ERA5-Land product provides 2-m temperature at a grid spacing of 0.1°, while the remaining environmental parameters and their associated ensemble spread are obtained from ERA5 reanalysis at a grid spacing of 0.25°. For each hailstorm, the grid point closest to the hailstorm center is first identified, and the surrounding eight grid points are also included to compute the environmental parameters.

To quantify uncertainty in the ERA5-based environmental analyses, we perform 1,000 Monte Carlo simulations. In each simulation, the environmental fields are perturbed by sampling from a normal distribution with a standard deviation given by the ERA5 ensemble spread. This procedure yields a range of p values and error bars, as shown in Fig. 3a–c.

Hailstorm analyses from observations and simulations
The results in Fig. 4a are calculated within a moving box of 200×200 km2 centered on hailstorms tracked using the program (examples included in the Code Availability section). Each hailstorm tracking result is temporally aligned with the first hail signal designated as time zero. The frequencies of convective initiation and cell merger in Fig. 4b are also derived using this program. The temperatures are averaged within the study areas.

Ten hailstorms near the New York city and ten hailstorms near the Pearl River Delta Region are selected to address the impact of AH effect on the genesis of hailstones (Supplementary Table 1). As an important additional heat source in urban canopy model, the AH participates the thermal balance in the simulations via the following processes74:

ρc_p V (dT_c/dt) = (X+Q_F,c)A_c, (1)

where ρ is the air density, c_p is the specific heat of air at constant pressure, V is air volume, T_c is air temperature, t is time, Q_F,c is the AH flux released, A_c is the bottom area of characterized buildings and street in canopy model, and X is other thermal variables. Thus, the AH flux directly contributes to the increase in near-surface temperatures, distinct from the radiative interactions of urban surface land cover. The distribution of AH flux in urban areas is uneven, depending on three subtypes of residential areas: low-density, high-density, and commercial residences. Each subtype exhibits diurnal variations, with two peaks at 08 and 17 LST (Supplementary Fig. 6c), reflecting levels of human activities such as traffic75,76.

High-resolution simulations are conducted using the Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF4.0). Two domains are used with 3 km and 1 km grid spacings (shown in Supplementary Fig. 6a–b) at an output interval of 5 minutes. Four groups of sensitivity experiments are independently conducted for each hailstorm case, only differing in the values of AH flux from 0 to 400 W/m2 (Supplementary Fig. 6c). The Milbrandt-Yau double-moment microphysical scheme is applied12. More information on model configuration is provided in Supplementary Table 2.

All results presented in Fig. 4c are calculated within a moving box of 200×200 km2 centered on the hail locations. The temperatures and CAPEs in Supplementary Fig. 7 are calculated specifically for urban areas. The updrafts and radar echoes are determined in regions where radar reflectivity exceeds 10 dBZ, which is considered the threshold for cloud cumulus formation77. The convective initiation (CI), cell merger (CM), and hail grid in Fig. 4c are derived within the study box. The frequency of CI and CM are obtained using the program (provided in the Code Availability section), while the hail grid is counted when grid points exceed 0.1 mm of accumulated hail at the surface.

Triple-hailfall storm analyses: radar data and retrievals
We conducted an in-depth analysis of a triple-hailfall event that occurred near the Pearl River Delta Region on March 19, 2016 (Supplementary Figs. 9–14). This event was selected as it featured two distinct hail formation mechanisms including merger pathway and normal pathway, providing a unique opportunity for the comparative analysis of hail growth processes under the consistent synoptic environments. Additionally, this event took place near a megacity, where ample observations enable robust cross-validation of urban effects on hailstorm evolution.

Three S-band radar observations were collected to analyze the structure and evolution of the storm under study, including one polarimetric radar (Supplementary Fig. 9). The three radars operate in the VCP21 mode consisting nine elevations (0.5°, 1.5°, 2.4°, 3.4°, 4.3°, 6.0°, 9.9°, 14.6°, and 19.5°). Radar reflectivities and three-dimensional wind fields are retrieved and interpolated onto a Cartesian Coordinate system with 1-km horizontal and 0.5-km vertical resolution using the NCAR LROSE software (https://www.eol.ucar.edu/software/lrose-core). Hydrometeor classification (Supplementary Figs. 10–11) was conducted based on the polarimetric radar variables using an updated S-band fuzzy logic algorithm (https://github.com/CSU-Radarmet/CSU_RadarTools). All variables in the first plot of Fig. 4d and supplementary Fig. 12 are calculated within a moving 60×60 km2 box centered on this hailstorm.

Two sensitivity experiments of AH4 and AH0 are set with a peak value of anthropogenic heat flux of 400 and 0 W/m2. The results presented in the latter two plots of Fig. 4d are derived from model outputs, including radar reflectivity (dBZ, shadings), updrafts (m/s, green contours), and hail content (g/kg, white contours).

Triple-hailfall storm analyses: hail trajectory model
Hail growth trajectories in Supplementary Fig. 13 are derived from observational retrievals using dual-Doppler wind method, calculated retrospectively by positioning hailstones within the storm at various heights. The dual-Doppler method utilizes radial velocities from at least two radars to retrieve the three-dimensional wind fields through an iterative process based on the equation of mass conservation78. The hailstone sizes are estimated using polarimetric variables from observations79.

To focus on reasonably possible hail trajectories, simplified assumptions are applied in this study. After testing several hail growth models, three fundamental equations are selected for the growth of hail particles80. The diffusional growth rate of hailstones is negligible compared to the accretional growth rate; hence, the mass growth equation is:

dm/dt = A_T V_T LWC, (2)

where m (kg) is the mass of hailstones, A_T (m2) is the cross-sectional area of a particle and LWC (kg/m3) is the cloud liquid water content derived from the sounding data81; V_T (m/s) is the particle terminal velocity, determined by the radius R (m) of hail particles82:

V_T = 485.2×R^0.8. (3)

The shape of particles is considered to be spherical and no melting process is included, hence the mass-diameter equation83 is formulated as:

m = 27905×R^3.53. (4)

For melting process, the mass equation is taken84 as:

(1/(c_w T + L_f)) dm/dt = -χ 2πR N_Re N_Pr (k_a T + N_Sc L_v Δρ_v a_v), when T > 0. (5)

Corresponding descriptions of these variables are listed in Supplementary Table 3. The storm-relative wind fields are further interpolated onto the storm-center coordinate every 1 minute. We aim to trace the origin of hail particles, emphasizing the impacts of merger process on hailstone genesis before melting. Accordingly, terminal hailstones are positioned at varying heights above the melting layer (about 4 km) at 18:48 LST and tracked backward using a 10s-time step. When hail particles descend below the melting layer, the melting process is calculated forward shaping hailstones prior to the landing on the surface. The hailstone trajectory model is provided in Code Availability section.

Hailstorm projections
Future hailstorm projections are conducted utilizing an advanced machine learning model, CatBoost, based on a dataset of 3,118 surface hail reports and 17 environmental parameters across North America. By training this model on current hailstorm occurrences under present mesoscale environmental conditions, we can project the future hailstorm occurrences in relation to climate trends. The process for making future hailstorm projections consists of four primary steps.

Step One: building the training dataset. We collected 2,082 surface hail reports of MHs and 1,036 records of NHs across North America (verified aforementioned). We select 17 mesoscale environmental parameters from ERA5 reanalysis which are commonly recognized as important for severe weather development and accessible from CMIP6 dataset simultaneously. These parameters include temperature (at multiple layers), specific humidity (at multiple layers), instability (CAPE), and wind shear (at various layers), as detailed in Supplementary Table 4. For each surface hail report, we identified the spatially nearest point within a 2-hour time window from two hours prior to the hail signal using the hourly ERA5 reanalysis at the horizontal resolution of 0.25°. This temporally expanded approach increases the sample size, allowing us to train a more precise model. Consequently, the training sample size for MHs is 2,082×3=6,246 and the sample size for NHs is 1,036×3=3,108 (Supplementary Table 4). Next, we establish a time window from 24 hours to 3 hours before the hail signal to create training samples for no hailstorms. We excluded any grid points with convection (> 40 dBZ) within 0.5° longitude/latitude radius. This process yielded a total of 46,446 samples for no hailstorms (see Supplementary Table 4).

Step Two: training the CatBoost model. CatBoost is an advanced decision tree-based model that uses gradient boosting algorithm to calculate the importance score of each contributing feature during training (https://catboost.ai/). CatBoost stands out due to its advanced architectures, including symmetric trees and ordered target encoding, which help reduce prediction bias and overfitting. These features collectively enhance the model’s accuracy with each training iteration. As a result, CatBoost generally outperforms traditional random forest models85,86 in weather prediction. In this study, the CatBoost model predicts three categorical features of MHs, NHs, and no hailstorms. This model is provided in Code Availability section. The dataset is split into sample sizes of 80% for training to 20% for testing, respectively (see Supplementary Table 5). The trained model achieves a high overall prediction accuracy of 96.85% on the testing data, indicating strong robustness and consistency across various computational environments. Detailed evaluation metrics are presented in Supplementary Table 5. Interpretability of machine learning model is as important as their predictive performance. To assess the importance of each environmental parameter, we employ the permutation importance method, which quantifies the global influence of individual features by measuring the performance degradation when their values are randomly shuffled87. The results are provided in Supplementary Fig. 15.

Step Three: building the CMIP6 environmental dataset. There are notable discrepancies between ERA5 and CMIP6 in terms of underlying physical processes, output variables, and spatiotemporal resolution. Hence, it is inappropriate to directly use CMIP6 outputs to predict hailstorm occurrence with the CatBoost model, which is trained on mesoscale environments derived from ERA5. To bridge the gap between climate scale of MCIP6 and mesoscale characteristics captured in ERA5, we use the training samples of environmental parameters from Step One as a baseline, and then extrapolate the mesoscale environments based on projected climate change trends. For example, if CMIP6 indicates that the average 2-m temperature increases by 0.4 °C during 2020–2024 compared to 2015–2019, we assume that the mesoscale 2-m temperatures will also increase by 0.4 °C on average. This approach captures the climate change trends while maintaining consistency between historical and projected mesoscale environmental conditions. However, this method does not fully capture the spatiotemporal variability of climate changes. As such, this work primarily focuses on average trends in projected hailstorm occurrences.

Step Four: hailstorm projections under future scenarios. Using the trained CatBoost model from Step Two and future mesoscale environmental conditions in Step Three, we can project future hailstorm occurrence. This study examines four future scenarios (i.e., SSP126, SSP245, SSP370, and SSP585) from three climate models (BCC-CSM2, CAS-ESM2, NorESM2). Each model provides monthly average atmospheric data with an approximate spatial resolution of 100 km. The results presented in Fig. 5 are aggregated from the three models for each future scenario.

Review of “Increased Hailstorms in Cities through Cell Merger Mechanism across North America and East Asia” submitted to Nature Communications.
This is an interesting study about the urbanization impact on hail frequency. The authors put a lot of effort in conducting observational analysis and model simulations. It should be a very nice study for a domain science journal. There is a significant science gap to meet the standards of the high-impact journals in my view.
1. Hail production and frequency are strongly related to aerosol environment and cloud microphysical processes. However, aerosol impact and cloud microphysics are neglected in this study. Besides the impact on thermodynamic environment, urbanization elevated aerosol concentration a lot, which can significantly enhance hail frequency, as shown from literature studies. While urbanization increases near-surface temperature, it also induces drying due to reduced latent heat fluxes, which might not strengthen storm, particularly may not favor the formation of condensates including hail in the storms. In my view, the increased aerosol concentrations from the cities can be a significant factor contributing to the increased hail frequency. But observational analysis and WRF model simulations did not consider this factor. In the WRF model simulations, the cloud microphysical scheme employed in the model is not even mentioned. This is important because some schemes do not even consider hail microphysics.
2. Another significant problem is the future hail frequency estimates. Future hailstorm projections using the environmental conditions from CIMP6 climate models is very problematic. This has been the common knowledge in the community. The science has been advanced to the state that convection permitting model simulations are needed to study the environmental factor impacts on hailstorms. Also, future aerosol impacts are not considered. As in the future, aerosol concentrations are likely less thus could reduce hail frequency. I think such crude estimate does not help the science advance (it is going backwards). This study can be better off without this part which has too large uncertainty.
3. Third, the environmental conditions analysis is problematic. “The environmental conditions in Fig. 3 are averaged based on the ERA5 reanalysis from 3 hours prior to the emergence of hail signature for every hailstorm event” – the method should not be appropriate. First the meteorological conditions from environment for a convective storm should be from the time before the convective initiation. Three hours prior to the emergence of hail signature could be in the middle of the convective system, which would not be representing the environment for convective initiation. Also, note that ERA5 data might not have the resolution high enough to distinguish urban and rural cases, and have large biases.
